title: The Battle of Uhud
subtitle: The Discipline of Archers, the Turning Tide, and the Shield Around the Messenger
summary: Tactical deployment at Mount Uhud, the strict command given to the fifty archers on Jabal al-Rumat, initial Muslim triumph, the fateful desertion for spoils, Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry encirclement, the martyrdom of Hamzah and Mus'ab, the fierce defense around the wounded Prophet, and rallying upon the mountain slopes.

sections.text: The Tactical Disposition and the Archers' Post

At sunrise on Saturday, the seventh of Shawwal in the third year after the Hijrah (March 625 CE), the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ deployed his seven hundred men at the foot of Mount Uhud. With brilliant military acumen, he positioned his army with the jagged, impassable red-granite massif of Uhud guarding their rear, while facing the open plain toward Madinah. To secure their vulnerable left flank—a low pass through which the superior Makkan cavalry could sweep around to strike from behind—the Prophet stationed a dedicated unit of fifty expert archers atop a rocky mound known as Jabal Aynayn (later famously called Jabal al-Rumat, the Mountain of Archers).
Appointing Abdullah ibn Jubayr as their commander, the Prophet gave the archers strict, unambiguous, and absolute orders, emphasizing their role as the linchpin of the army's survival:

احْمُوا ظُهُورَنَا، فَإِنْ رَأَيْتُمُونَا نُخْطَفُ فَلَا تَنْزِلُوا، وَإِنْ رَأَيْتُمُونَا ظَهَرْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فَلَا تَبْرَحُوا حَتَّى أُرْسِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ
'Protect our backs! If you see us being snatched away by birds, do not abandon your post; and if you see us defeat the enemy and trample upon them, do not leave your post until I send word to you!' (Sahih al-Bukhari)
The rocky mound of Jabal al-Rumat overlooking the battlefield of Uhud.
Initial Muslim Victory

The battle opened with ferocious intensity. Talhah ibn Abi Talhah, standard-bearer of Quraysh, stepped forward challenging any Muslim to duel; Ali ibn Abi Talib charged out and struck him down with a single blow. One by one, ten champion standard-bearers of Banu Abd al-Dar took up the Makkan banner, only to be slain in succession by Ali and Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, until the banner fell to the dust with no one daring to lift it.

Led by the fierce charges of Hamzah, Ali, and Abu Dujanah—who fought wearing the Prophet's red headband of death—the Muslim infantry shattered the Makkan center. The enemy broke in wild disorder, fleeing across the plain toward their encampment. The Muslim warriors pursued them into their tents, capturing baggage and spoils, while Makkan women dropped their tambourines and fled up the rocky hills.
The Fatal Error on the Ridge

Watching the enemy flee from their elevated vantage point atop Jabal al-Rumat, the archers witnessed their comrades collecting gold, carpets, and armor in the abandoned camp. Human weakness overtook their discipline. The cry arose among them: 'The spoils! The spoils! Our companions have triumphed, why should we stand idle?'

Their commander, Abdullah ibn Jubayr, shouted desperately: 'Have you forgotten what the Messenger of God commanded you?' But forty of the fifty archers disregarded his pleas and rushed down the slope to claim their share of the booty, leaving fewer than ten men defending the vital pass.

Khalid ibn al-Walid, commanding the Makkan right cavalry, was a military genius who had been probing the pass for hours. Spotting the hill suddenly deserted, Khalid executed a brilliant tactical maneuver: wheeled his two hundred cavalry around the rear of Uhud, overran and martyred Abdullah ibn Jubayr and his small band, and crashed into the rear of the dispersed Muslim army. Amrah bint Alqamah lifted the fallen Makkan banner, rally cries erupted, and the routed Makkans turned back. In an instant, the Muslims were trapped in a deadly vice between two enemy forces.
The rugged crags of Mount Uhud where the wounded companions rallied around the Prophet.
Chaos, Martyrdom, and the Living Shield

Confusion engulfed the battlefield. In the blinding dust, Muslims inadvertently struck one another. It was during this chaos that the beloved uncle of the Prophet, Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib (the Lion of God), was martyred. Wahshi ibn Harb, an Ethiopian slave promised freedom by Hind bint Utbah if he slew Hamzah, hurled his javelin from behind a boulder, striking Hamzah mortally through the lower abdomen. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, the heroic standard-bearer of Islam, was also slain while defending his post.

Because Mus'ab bore a striking physical resemblance to the Prophet, his killer Ibn Qami'ah shrieked triumphantly across the valley: 'Muhammad is killed!' The devastating rumor paralyzed many believers; some dropped their weapons in despair, while others, like Anas ibn al-Nadr, charged into the fray shouting: 'What will you do with life after him? Rise and die for that which the Messenger of God died!' Anas fought until he fell with over eighty wounds.

In reality, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ remained alive, surrounded by a tiny circle of approximately a dozen companions who formed a human shield of unbelievable valor. Talhah ibn Ubaydillah shielded the Prophet with his own chest, intercepting incoming arrows until his hand was permanently paralyzed. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shot arrows with deadly accuracy as the Prophet handed them to him, saying: 'Shoot, O Sa'd! May my father and mother be sacrificed for you!' Nusaybah bint Ka'b (Umm Umarah) fought fiercely with sword and bow, sustaining twelve wounds while defending the Messenger of God.
The Injury of the Prophet and the Mountain Sanctuary

Despite this heroic defense, enemy strikes reached the Prophet ﷺ. Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas cast stones that split his lower lip and chipped his right incisor tooth, while Ibn Qami'ah struck his face with a heavy sword stroke, driving two iron rings of his helmet deep into his cheekbone. Blood streamed down his noble face as he wiped it away, whispering with sublime forbearance: 'How can a people prosper who wound their Prophet's face and break his tooth while he calls them to their Lord?'

Ka'b ibn Malik was the first to recognize the Prophet alive beneath his helmet, shouting at the top of his voice: 'O Muslims, rejoice! Here is the Messenger of God!' Believers rallied to his call. Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah extracted the two embedded helmet rings with his teeth, breaking two of his own incisors in the process. Ali ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah washed the wound and burned a piece of straw matting to staunch the bleeding. Forming a disciplined phalanx, the companions withdrew the Prophet up the narrow, rocky defiles of Mount Uhud, where the enemy cavalry could not follow, bringing the traumatic battle to an end.
